CS 301 · Meeting 13 · Recap 1

Lines, Planes, and a Walk

Linear systems, their geometric solutions, sensitivity to changes in the data, and a random walk on a graph.

A linear system in matrix form

2x+y=5,x−y=1⟹A=[211−1], x=[xy], b=[51]
  • Linear: a sum of unknowns multiplied by coefficients
  • One row per equation; A @ x evaluates their left-hand sides
  • np.linalg.solve(A, b): the x that makes A @ x == b
Notes. A linear equation is a sum of unknowns multiplied by coefficients. A system consists of equations that must hold together. Each row of A contains the coefficients of one equation, so A @ x evaluates the left-hand sides. Solving finds x such that A @ x equals b. The first thinking cell asked students to explain this notation for a thousand equations.

Elimination, by hand

2x+y=5x−y=1add: 3x=6 ⇒ x=2, y=1
  • Use one equation to remove an unknown from the other
  • Substitute the value back to find the other unknown
  • solve uses elimination in compiled code
Notes. Add the equations to eliminate y, solve for x, and substitute back to find y. Gaussian elimination applies this procedure to larger systems. The second notebook implements it with loops and counts the operations.

An equation is a line; the solution is where lines cross

  • All the points (x, y) that satisfy one equation: a line
  • A solution satisfies both: a point on both lines
Notes. Each line consists of the points that satisfy one equation. A solution lies on both lines. Two nonparallel lines cross once, giving a unique solution. Students entered the second system themselves (3x + 2y = 12, x - 4y = -10). The check identifies swapped rows and columns and a missing sign.

Three unknowns: three planes, one point

  • An equation in three unknowns: a plane
  • Here, two planes meet along a line; the third selects one point
Notes. The notebook uses an interactive plotly figure; this slide shows a fixed view. In this example, the first two planes intersect along a line and the third intersects that line at one point. These three independent equations therefore have a unique solution.

When the third plane adds nothing

NumPy refuses the system: Singular matrix
Correct: the three equations hold only 2 independent ones, and the planes share a line.
  • The third equation = the first + the second: rank 2, not 3
  • Infinitely many solutions; with another right-hand side, none
Notes. The groups replaced the third equation by the sum of the first two. The third plane then contains the whole line of the first two, every point of the line is a solution, and NumPy refuses: Singular matrix. The rank of A is the number of linearly independent coefficient rows; a square system has one solution exactly when its rank is n. With another right-hand side, 12 for 11, the third plane is parallel to the line and misses it: no solution, and the same error. Both cases exist with two lines too: the same line twice, or two parallel lines.

Nearly parallel: the condition number

lines that cross at a right angle:
   the solution [1. 1.], after the change [1.0005 0.9995]: moved by 0.0007
   condition number 1
lines that are nearly parallel:
   the solution [1. 1.], after the change [0. 2.]: moved by 1.4142
   condition number 4,002
Notes. Both systems have solution (1, 1). A change of one thousandth in b moves the first solution by 0.0007 and the second by 1.4. Nearly parallel lines can have an intersection that moves substantially under a small shift. The condition number bounds the amplification of relative changes in b: it is 1 for the first system and about 4,000 for the second. Students then brought the second row close to the first to obtain a condition number of at least a million.

Conditioning and reliable digits

condition numberrelative-error amplificationdigits retained, worst-case estimate
1at most 1×16
10⁴up to 10,000 timesabout 12
10⁸up to 10⁸ timesabout 8
10¹²up to 10¹² timesabout 4
10¹⁶up to 10¹⁶ timesnone
  • Worst-case estimate: potential digits ≈ max(0, 16 − log₁₀(condition number))
  • Six-digit data, condition number 10⁶: no reliable digits guaranteed
  • Use np.linalg.cond(A) to assess sensitivity
Notes. With about 16 digits of floating-point precision, a condition number of 10^k can cost up to k digits. This is an estimate of potential loss; the actual error depends on the perturbation. The third thinking cell asks how nearly parallel lines affect a solution computed from measured data. A small residual alone does not establish accuracy: interpret it together with the condition number.

A walk on a graph

  • From each node: a random neighbour, again and again, until red or blue
  • 2,000 walks from each node: the fraction that reached red first
Notes. A particle starts at a node and moves to a uniformly chosen neighbour until it reaches red or blue. The notebook simulates 2,000 walks from each node. Students propose an equation relating a non-boundary node’s true hitting probability to its neighbours’ probabilities. The simulated fractions are estimates. Introduce the web example here: two parties have pages connected by links, and a reader follows links at random. Which party’s page does the reader reach first?

The equations for the walk

xv=1deg(v)∑u~vxufor every other node,xred=1, xblue=0
node 6 has the neighbours [8, 13, 14]: its equation is x6 = (x8 + x13 + x14) / 3
the row of node 6 in the matrix: 1 at column 6, -0.333 at column 8, -0.333 at column 13, -0.333 at column 14, 0 elsewhere
  • One probability per node: 16 unknowns and 16 equations
  • deg(v), the degree of v: its number of neighbours
  • Average the neighbours’ probabilities after the first step
Notes. Let x_v be the probability that a walk from v reaches red first. It is 1 at red and 0 at blue. From another node, the first step chooses each neighbour with probability one over the degree. Conditioning on that step gives x_v as the average of the neighbours’ probabilities. These are sixteen linear equations, which np.linalg.solve solves directly. The printed matrix row represents a node of degree 3: 1 on the diagonal and -1/3 in each neighbour’s column.

Direct solution and 2,000 simulated walks

largest difference between the 2,000 walks and the exact solution: 0.032

 node  neighbours  simulated   exact
    0           7       0.37   0.363
    1           6       0.22   0.227
    2           5       0.29   0.265
    3           5       0.58   0.600
  • The simulation approximates the probabilities found by solve
Notes. Compare the directly computed probabilities with the simulation estimates. With 2,000 trials, sampling error is typically on the order of a few hundredths. Solving the 16 equations avoids that sampling error, though floating-point round-off remains. Large graphs require suitable storage and solvers. Ask which proposals in the posts match the averaging equations.
